note: The one specification for §6's gift fields. `backend/tests/gift.test.ts` and
`storefront/tests/gift.test.ts` both read this file, so a rule that changes in
one workspace and not the other fails on the side that did not move.
`addresses` is the half unique to gifting: the recipient's address is validated
rather than sanitised, because §5's filter exists to remove things that look
like addresses and running it here would reject every valid input.
`text` reuses §5's filter through `sanitiseInscription`, so the cases here are
the ones that matter *for a gift* rather than a second copy of
`inscription-cases.json`. The argument is not publicity — none of these fields
is published — but that this slice sends attacker-supplied text to an
arbitrary address over our own DKIM signature.

addresses.why: surrounding whitespace is trimmed, not rejected
a plus tag is a real address and a common one
no domain dot, so not routable
two addresses; a comma is how a second recipient arrives
angle brackets, which is how a header is injected
a display name in front of it, same reason
an embedded newline, the classic header injection

text.input: Someone spent five dollars so you would not have to
text.output: Someone spent five dollars so you would not have to

text.why: a URL is what makes this a spam vector, and it goes
a bare domain goes too, since it is a link a reader will type
an address in the body would be a reply-to we did not choose
a telephone number goes; §5's rule, and a gift is no different
markup goes, because the message reaches an HTML body
a script element goes with its contents, not just its tags
a message that was entirely a URL leaves nothing, and null is the no-message state
a quantity keeps its digits; §5's Gate D finding, and it applies here
empty is the no-message state, not an empty message
